2.note: The word translated as **For** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [This is because]

By **the seas** and **the rivers** David means the waters that existed before God created the dry land. David, and people in his culture, thought of the world as being founded and placed by God upon subterranean waters. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [For he has founded it upon the waters that were there before creation] or [For he has founded it upon the deep waters under the earth]

3.note: David is using questions to cause his readers to think deeply about who is qualified to approach God. David is not asking for information, but is emphasizing that only people who meet certain requirements can approach God. If you would not use rhetorical questions for this purpose in your language, you could translate his questions as statements or exclamations. Alternate translation: [Only certain people may ascend on the mountain of Yahweh! Only certain people may stand in his holy place!]

David assumes that readers will know that **the mountain of Yahweh** and **his holy place** refer to Mount Zion in Jerusalem, where the Tabernacle of Yahweh was located. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Who may ascend Mount Zion, the mountain of Yahweh? And who may stand in his holy Tabernacle]

4.note: David is using the possessive form to describe **one** that is characterized by **clean of hands and pure of heart**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [The one who has clean hands and a pure heart]

Here, **hands** represents a person’s actions or conduct. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [The one whose actions are clean and whose heart is pure] or [The one who acts righteously]

In this image, the **heart** represents a person’s thoughts, feelings, and motives, and David speaks of them as if they could be physically clean. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and whose thoughts are pure] or [and whose motives are pure]

David is using the term **soul** to mean the entire person from the perspective of his spiritual and emotional existence. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [who has not devoted himself to falsehood] or [who has not set his heart to worship idols] or [who has not set his heart to worship what is false]
David assumes that readers will know that **what is false** refers to idol worship. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [to idols]

5.note: The implication is that the person described in the previous verse will receive these things from God. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [He will receive]

5.q: יִשָּׂ֣א בְ֭רָכָה מֵ⁠אֵ֣ת יְהוָ֑ה וּ֝⁠צְדָקָ֗ה מֵ⁠אֱלֹהֵ֥י יִשְׁעֽ⁠וֹ
5.note: If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **blessing** and **righteousness** and **salvation**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [Yahweh will bless him and act righteously toward him; this is what the God who saves him will do for him]

By **and righteousness from the God of his salvation**, David means that God will vindicate this type of person by declaring that they are righteous. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and vindication from the God of his salvation] or [and God will vindicate this person by declaring him righteous]
See how you translated the similar phrase “the God of my salvation” in 18:46. Alternate translation: [from the God who saves him]

6.note: Here, **generation** represents a type or class of people who have something in common. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [This is the kind of people who seek him] or [These are the people who seek him]

These two phrases **the ones seeking him** and **the ones seeking your face** mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [the ones seeking him, yes, the ones seeking your face]

Here, **face** represents God’s presence. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the ones seeking to be in your presence] or [the ones seeking to know you intimately]

Here, **Jacob** represents the people of Israel, who are the descendants of Jacob and who sought God’s favor like Jacob did. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the people of Israel] or [the descendants of Jacob]

7.q: שְׂא֤וּ שְׁעָרִ֨ים ׀ רָֽאשֵׁי⁠כֶ֗ם וְֽ֭⁠הִנָּשְׂאוּ פִּתְחֵ֣י עוֹלָ֑ם
7.note: These two phrases **Lift up your heads, you gates** and **be lifted up, you ancient doors** mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [Lift up your heads, you gates, yes, be lifted up, you ancient doors]

7.q: שְׂא֤וּ שְׁעָרִ֨ים ׀ רָֽאשֵׁי⁠כֶ֗ם וְֽ֭⁠הִנָּשְׂאוּ פִּתְחֵ֣י עוֹלָ֑ם
7.note: Here the words **gates** and **doors** could refer to: (1) the gates leading into Yahweh’s Tabernacle on Mount Zion. Alternate translation: [Lift up your heads, you Tabernacle gates, and be lifted up, you ancient doors], or (2) the gates leading into the city of Jerusalem. Alternate translation: [Lift up your heads, you city gates, and be lifted up, you ancient doors]

7.q: שְׂא֤וּ שְׁעָרִ֨ים ׀ רָֽאשֵׁי⁠כֶ֗ם וְֽ֭⁠הִנָּשְׂאוּ פִּתְחֵ֣י עוֹלָ֑ם
7.note: David is speaking of the **gates** and **doors** that led into Yahweh’s Tabernacle as if they were living things that could lift up their heads. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Open wide the Tabernacle gates]

The expression **be lifted up** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and lift yourselves up, you ancient doors] or [and you gatekeepers, lift up the ancient doors]

David is using this possessive form to mean a king who has glory or a king who is glorious. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [so that the glorious king may come in]
In a context such as this, your language might say “go” instead of **come**. Alternate translation: [so that the King of glory may go in]

8.note: David is using the question **Who is this King of glory?** to introduce and emphasize the answer that follows. This is not a request for information, but a way to draw attention to Yahweh’s identity and attributes. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could express this as a statement or an exclamation. Alternate translation: [This is the King of glory] or [I will tell you who this King of glory is]
See how you translated the phrase **King of glory** in the previous verse. Alternate translation: [Who is this glorious king]

The terms **strong** and **mighty** mean similar things. David is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. [Yahweh, who is very strong] or [Yahweh, the powerful one]

9.q: שְׂא֤וּ שְׁעָרִ֨ים ׀ רָֽאשֵׁי⁠כֶ֗ם וּ֭⁠שְׂאוּ פִּתְחֵ֣י עוֹלָ֑ם וְ֝⁠יָבֹא מֶ֣לֶךְ הַ⁠כָּבֽוֹד
9.note: Here David is speaking of **gates** and **doors** as if they were people who could lift up their heads. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express this meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Open wide, you gates, and open wide, you ancient doors, so that the King of glory may come in]

10.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 24:8.

David is using this possessive form to mean that Yahweh is the commander of **armies** (the army of Israel and the army of heaven made of up angels). It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Yahweh, the commander of armies] or [Yahweh, who commands armies]
